title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: miniTE : Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39 × \times and 1.47 × \times the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning is central to large language model (LLM) post-training, supporting instruction following ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) and mathematical reasoning ( Shao et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Repeated generation, policy evaluation, and updates ( Yu et al., 2026 ) span an autoregressive sampler and a learner that optimizes on sampled sequences. Native low-precision computation must accelerate these engines while preserving effective learning. Four-bit weight storage ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) and native four-bit training ( Castro et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) address different execution paths. Quantized sampling, matched precision, and quantization-aware RL address learner–sampler mismatch ( Huang and others, 2025 ; Xi et al., 2026 ; Zhuge et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) ; recent systems also support per-token NVFP4 and high-precision backward ( Cursor Research, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . We focus on native weight-and-activation four-bit (W4A4) expert computation, connecting cross-engine diagnosis, a practical numerical path, and complete learner gains. RL makes cross-engine numerical behavior consequential. Probabilities computed by the learner and sampler enter importance ratios and clipping decisions ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) ; implementation differences therefore enter optimization even at a shared parameter version. Training–inference mismatch and execution-aligned references have been studied in RL pipelines ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) . NVFP4 adds choices in scale domains, rounding, accumulation, and operator composition that a format name does not specify. This raises a concrete question: which numerical dependencies must be exposed and controlled when native low-bit computation spans two execution engines? Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models combine continuous expert computation with discrete routing. Selective router precision and routing replay address sensitivity in expert selection ( Fedus et al., 2022 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . We examine what remains after controlling parameter updates and matching assignments at the observed layer. Frozen-policy scoring shows that NVFP4 enlarges the cross-engine log-probability tail. Target-layer routing agreement leaves FC1/FC2 output discrepancies, and a sampler-only scaling change does not establish agreement (Figure 1 ). These controls identify an execution specification, extending beyond bit width and expert IDs, as a useful unit of diagnosis and implementation. Motivated by these findings, we introduce miniTE to connect this diagnosis with practical native NVFP4 training (Figure 2 ). Our framework checks quantized operands, expert outputs, and policy evaluation across the sampler and learner. Strict execution provides a cross-engine reference for diagnosis; the default path combines our per-token quantization and native grouped-GEMM implementation with BF16 backward. Its purpose is stable, high-throughput learning under the existing RL objective. Arithmetic throughput is only one component of this cost: routed expert workloads also require operand preparation, representation conversion, and dispatch. We therefore optimize quantization and grouped GEMM as a connected dataflow, reducing repeated preparation around the numerical core so that FP4 arithmetic gains translate into faster learner updates. Comparisons between our initial and optimized operator implementations check the numerical effects of those changes. Long-horizon Qwen3-30B-A3B runs show sustained learning with miniTE and higher mathematical evaluation scores than naive NVFP4. Same-recipe module comparisons show 2.46 × 2.46\times expert-forward speedup over TE U3045. Complete learner updates on fixed text reach 1.39 × 1.39\times BF16 throughput in the optimized configuration and 1.33 × 1.33\times in a repeated core study. The module comparison measures native implementation gains; complete learner updates measure the numerical path and implementation together. Separate colocated RL measurements identify weight conversion and synchronization as an integration bottleneck. Our contributions are: 1. Execution-gap diagnosis. Frozen-policy, routing-conditioned, and scaling controls identify numerical differences beyond nominal NVFP4 recipe agreement; strict execution supplies an actionable alignment reference. 2. Practical native NVFP4 RL. An integrated W4A4 expert-forward path with BF16 backward sustains long-horizon learning and improves all four mathematics benchmarks over naive NVFP4 without modifying the RL objective. 3. A lightweight framework with numerically faithful acceleration. miniTE exposes configurable numerical recipes, replaceable expert operators, and reusable diagnostics for developing custom low-bit training settings. Operator-level numerical checks and complete learner benchmarks substantiate its execution optimizations. We release Dockerfiles, reference configurations, and single-command launch scripts to support reproducible experiments and extensions across the supported low-bit RL paths.

sections.heading: What NVFP4 fixes.
sections.text: NVFP4 combines E2M1 values with one E4M3 scale per block of 16 values and an outer FP32 scale ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . For a nonzero block b b , outer scale g g , and block maximum a b = max i ∈ b ⁡ | x i | a_{b}=\max_{i\in b}|x_{i}| , its reconstruction is s b = E4M3 ⁡ ( a b 6 ​ g ) , c i = E2M1 ⁡ ( x i g ​ s b ) , x ^ i = g ​ s b ​ c i . s_{b}=\operatorname{E4M3}\!\left(\frac{a_{b}}{6g}\right),\qquad c_{i}=\operatorname{E2M1}\!\left(\frac{x_{i}}{gs_{b}}\right),\qquad\hat{x}_{i}=gs_{b}c_{i}. (3) Here 6 is the largest E2M1 magnitude. If a rounded block scale is zero, the implementation sets its codes to zero. The outer scale can cover an entire tensor or a row. Row-wise scaling reduces dependence on maxima in other rows and changes how block scales use the E4M3 dynamic range. It does not fix rounding instructions, reduction order, padding, or where router weights and output casts enter the computation. Those choices are part of the execution specification.

sections.heading: Three comparisons.
sections.text: We distinguish quantization error (NVFP4 versus BF16 within a stack), cross-stack execution difference (learner versus sampler), and implementation difference (optimized versus reference code for the same operator). Frozen-policy evaluation measures cross-stack execution difference; reference-implementation tests measure the effect of an optimization; training and benchmark evaluation measure learning quality. Throughout, native W4A4 refers to the expert-forward GEMMs. Attention, non-expert modules, backward, and optimizer state retain their specified higher precisions.

sections.heading: 3  Diagnosing the Execution Gap
sections.text: The frozen-policy study scores identical token sequences under teacher forcing with a frozen Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base checkpoint ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . Tails use 32 prompts and 69,088 matched tokens; localization uses 12 prompts at 11 depths. Confidence intervals use 2,000 prompt-cluster bootstrap resamples. Within-stack self-comparisons are bitwise exact. Appendix C specifies the collectors and full protocol.

sections.heading: 3.1  Does the Gap Exist Before Optimization?
sections.text: The execution gap is already present at a shared, frozen parameter version. The P99 of | δ t num | |\delta^{\mathrm{num}}_{t}| increases from 0.1271 nats under BF16 to 0.2911 under NVFP4 (Figure 1 , left). The paired increase is 0.1641, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.1311, 0.2005]. NVFP4 therefore amplifies the log-probability tail beyond the BF16 cross-engine floor before any optimizer update takes place. Figure 1 : Execution differences survive recipe and routing agreement. Left: Frozen-policy absolute logp tails, displayed through pooled P99.9; statistics use all matched tokens. Right: FC1/FC2 discrepancies with matched target-layer assignments at all 11 depths and no invalid experts; inputs retain upstream differences. Shading: 95% prompt-cluster bootstrap intervals. Numerical-only ratios exceed the analysis clipping bounds for 1.203% of NVFP4 tokens versus 0.627% under BF16. This is clipping potential; training also depends on advantages, updates, and TIS correction. Appendix C reports the full statistics.

sections.heading: Matched routing leaves operator differences.
sections.text: We fix expert assignments at each target layer while retaining its naturally accumulated inputs. FC1 symmetric relative- L 2 L_{2} discrepancies range from 0.0381 to 0.6124, and FC2 discrepancies from 0.0810 to 0.7624 (Figure 1 , right). Matched assignments therefore leave residual output differences. Natural routing additionally shows changing expert selections and nonmonotonic depth-dependent divergence. A separate replay at a common MoE-layer input also leaves FC1/FC2 differences between learner modules and the sampler reference (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: Finer scales alone do not establish consistency.
sections.text: Changing only the sampler activation outer scale from per-tensor to per-token leaves FC1/FC2 discrepancies unchanged; the tail change is inconclusive on this four-prompt cohort. The early per-token candidate also retains a larger tail than standard NVFP4 (Appendix C ). These controls motivate specifying the complete operator path: finer scales alone do not establish cross-engine agreement.

sections.heading: Implication for the training path.
sections.text: These findings motivate specifying the operands and composition that define each execution. miniTE makes these choices explicit and implements a native training path, evaluated for learning behavior and cost in Section 5 .

sections.heading: 4 miniTE : A Practical Native NVFP4 RL Framework
sections.text: Section 3 motivates making the executed numerical path explicit. We choose a native recipe whose activation scales depend on each token row, and jointly optimize the cost of executing it. Figure 2 connects this numerical specification to diagnostic interfaces and the native expert-computation dataflow. Figure 2 : Numerical specification and efficient execution in miniTE . (a) Cross-engine comparisons at operand, expert-output, and policy boundaries, with a strict execution reference. (b) Packed W4A4 expert forward, FP32 epilogue rescaling, and BF16 backward on saved high-precision operands. Contiguous buffers, device metadata, and producer statistics connect quantization directly to grouped GEMM.

sections.heading: Operands and composition.
sections.text: An execution specification records scale domains, rounding, logical layouts, and the placement of casts and router coefficients. Comparisons fix the weight version, token IDs, and scoring context, then decode codes and scales to a common layout. Input provenance and expert IDs identify the comparison boundary: naturally accumulated inputs reveal cross-engine differences, while common-input comparisons test the operators applied at that boundary. This distinction follows directly from the residual differences under matched target-layer routing.

sections.heading: Two complementary references.
sections.text: The strict execution reference matches learner kernels, formulas, and reduction orders to the sampler, including surrounding normalization and communication paths. It retains native NVFP4 expert forward and BF16 gradients, and provides a cross-engine intervention evaluated in Section 5.4 . The operator reference instead compares initial and optimized implementations on common inputs under a fixed recipe. It tests whether an API or layout transformation preserves quantized operands and outputs. The practical learner below is evaluated as a complete learning configuration; its implementation checks use the latter reference.

sections.heading: Scaling with local activation dependence.
sections.text: Each dispatched activation row has its own outer scale, removing dependence on other tokens’ maxima under fixed quantization rules. This addresses token-grouping differences between learner and sampler at the quantizer boundary; weight scales, accumulation, and composition complete the numerical path. For expert e e , token t t , and weight output row n n , the row-wise native path uses the normal-range dequantization factors g e , t x = max k ⁡ | X e , t ​ k | 6 ⋅ 448 , g e , n w = max k ⁡ | W e , n ​ k | 6 ⋅ 448 . g^{x}_{e,t}=\frac{\max_{k}|X_{e,tk}|}{6\cdot 448},\qquad g^{w}_{e,n}=\frac{\max_{k}|W_{e,nk}|}{6\cdot 448}. (4) Length-16 E4M3 block scales and E2M1 codes follow Eq. ( 3 ). Hadamard transforms and stochastic rounding are disabled in this path. A context-swap test varies companion rows around fixed target rows. The tested miniTE path preserves target-row FP4 codes and GEMM outputs bitwise; the RHT-enabled per-tensor reference changes in five of six swaps.

sections.heading: Independent backward precision.
sections.text: The default backward uses a straight-through approximation with saved, original BF16 activations and weights. For upstream gradient G e G_{e} , BF16 GEMMs compute ∇ X e ≈ G e ​ W e \nabla X_{e}\approx G_{e}W_{e} and ∇ W e ≈ G e 𝖳 ​ X e \nabla W_{e}\approx G_{e}^{\mathsf{T}}X_{e} . This choice preserves high-precision operands for the gradient path while avoiding backward quantization and its preparation costs. Section 5.4 compares its complete forward-plus-backward cost with the MXFP8 alternative.

sections.heading: MoE composition and RL integration.
sections.text: The learner applies router probabilities to the SwiGLU activation before FC2, followed by expert combination. Padding, quantization, and casts preserve this order. Non-expert modules retain their configured higher precisions. Weight conversion and synchronization connect the learner to an NVFP4 sampler with per-token activation scaling; the existing TIS-corrected RL pipeline consumes their policy evaluations.

sections.heading: 4.3  Joint Design of Quantization and Grouped GEMM
sections.text: Routed expert computation requires operand preparation and scheduling in addition to matrix multiplication. Expert-dependent group sizes, empty groups, and padding affect the interface between these operations. We optimize that interface as a connected dataflow.

sections.heading: A shared producer–consumer representation.
sections.text: The reference quantizer already processes grouped inputs, but returns expert views or lists from which grouped GEMM reconstructs its arguments. miniTE writes packed FP4 codes, block scales, and outer-scale information directly into contiguous buffers consumed by GEMM. Device-side offsets describe expert boundaries, and metadata storage and workspaces are reused. This removes repeated splitting and argument preparation between two grouped interfaces while retaining expert-dependent offsets and padding, including support for empty groups.

sections.heading: Statistics travel with their activations.
sections.text: The FC1 reference permutes tokens, pads them, and scans the padded rows for maxima. miniTE collects maxima during permutation and pads both the activations and statistics: Reference : sort → pad ⁡ ( X ) → amax ​ scan → quant miniTE : sort + amax → pad ⁡ ( X , amax ) → quant \begin{array}[]{rcl}\text{Reference}&:&\mathrm{sort}\rightarrow\mathrm{pad}(X)\rightarrow\boxed{\mathrm{amax\ scan}}\rightarrow\mathrm{quant}\\[5.69054pt] \textsc{miniTE}&:&\boxed{\mathrm{sort}+\mathrm{amax}}\rightarrow\mathrm{pad}(X,\mathrm{amax})\rightarrow\mathrm{quant}\end{array} FC2 obtains maxima from the router-weighted activation producer, matching the tensor actually consumed by its quantizer. Joint handling of statistics and padding eliminates the extra activation scan without introducing a separate metadata-processing path. Producer-side statistics also appear in COAT’s group scaling ( Xi et al., 2025 ) ; here they cross MoE permutation, padding, weighted activation, and NVFP4’s two scale levels. Complete learner timing includes the producer’s work.

sections.heading: Layout and native GEMM execution.
sections.text: Fused scale layout preparation supplies the format consumed by Tensor Cores. FC1 and FC2 use GEMM configurations adapted to their different reduction lengths, coupling tile selection and tensor-memory allocation. The optimized path combines these choices with the dense representation, permutation fusion, and amax reuse. Sections 5.3 and 5.4 report implementation gains and numerical checks for these transformations; Appendix F gives configuration details.

sections.heading: Framework integration.
sections.text: Users integrate miniTE by replacing the expert grouped-linear module through a common expert-computation interface. Quantization recipes and backward precision are configurable separately, with BF16 and MXFP8 backward available for the supported NVFP4 paths. Compatible quantizer and grouped-GEMM implementations provide layout and scheduling options within the existing RL orchestration. The operand, expert-output, and policy-evaluation boundaries in Section 4.1 provide reusable comparison points for checking each recipe or kernel change.

sections.heading: 5  Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate learning behavior, complete learner efficiency, and the numerical and performance effects of the implementation design. The frozen comparisons in Section 3 establish the problem; the experiments here evaluate the training configurations and execution paths.

sections.heading: Model and configurations.
sections.text: We use Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base. The standard baseline uses TE’s per-tensor NVFP4 recipe on expert grouped linear layers ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) ; non-expert learner modules remain BF16. All non-strict RL arms use Truncated importance sampling (TIS). A separate strict reference evaluates joint execution alignment without TIS. Table 9 records the main RL and evaluation protocol; Appendix B identifies the implementations.

sections.heading: Complete learner updates.
sections.text: Timing uses eight B300 GPUs, sequence length 4,096, and global batch size 128: 524,288 tokens per update, including forward, backward, communication, and optimizer work. All configurations share a BF16 checkpoint, seed, and frozen DAPO-Math-17k workload ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . The core study uses ten process trials; the optimized study uses one, with two warm-up updates followed by 15 measurements, trimmed to 13. Appendix B specifies the workload and throughput estimators.

sections.heading: Module and routing controls.
sections.text: FC1 and FC2 use balanced expert workloads at four token counts, with five process trials per cell and warm unchanged weights. Forward and forward-plus-backward are measured directly. A separate eight-GB200 study crosses model initialization with input data to examine the routed workload (Appendix G ).

sections.heading: 5.2  Long-Horizon Training Behavior and Evaluation
sections.text: Figure 3 compares BF16, naive NVFP4+TIS, and miniTE +TIS through recorded log-probability discrepancy and reward over the first 1,000 steps. miniTE maintains reward growth and achieves higher late-run reward than the standard NVFP4 trace, while BF16 reaches higher reward over that region. The two NVFP4 paths have similar mean log-probability discrepancies despite their different reward trajectories. Thus the observed learning behavior is evaluated for the complete recipe; the mean training metric alone does not identify which numerical differences affect learning. Figure 3 : Learning with native NVFP4 and TIS. (a) Absolute learner–sampler logp difference; (b) reward. Each configuration contributes one run. Faint curves show raw values; solid curves show centered 21-step means. Insets magnify marked regions. Appendix E.1 gives endpoints and plotting details.

sections.heading: Complete updates.
sections.text: These measurements cover complete learner updates on fixed text, rather than end-to-end RL iterations. The optimized miniTE path reaches 33,540 tokens/s, or 1.39 × 1.39\times BF16 and 1.47 × 1.47\times TE NVFP4 throughput (Table 2 ). The repeated core study reaches 32,517 tokens/s and a trial-ID-paired trimmed speedup of 1.334 × 1.334\times over BF16. The optimized setting combines the dense path, FC1/FC2 GEMM configuration, permutation fusion, and activation-amax reuse. These measurements establish the cost of that combined numerical and execution configuration. The 1.334 × 1.334\times core estimate averages paired speedup ratios after trimming; dividing its aggregate throughputs instead gives 1.344 × 1.344\times . sections.heading: Implementation gain under the same forward recipe.
sections.text: Relative to the pinned upstream per-token implementation (TE U3045), miniTE accelerates expert forward by a geometric mean of 2.46 × 2.46\times across FC1/FC2 and four workload sizes, ranging from 1.587 × 1.587\times to 3.065 × 3.065\times . This comparison measures the implementation and interface gains at the expert-module boundary under a common forward recipe. Complete-update comparisons measure the numerical recipe and surrounding execution together. Module inputs are pre-permuted, dispatch is excluded, and FC2 starts from an activation prepared outside the timer. The module and learner gains therefore have different references and timing boundaries. The full latency grid is in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Why realistic routed workloads matter.
sections.text: Balanced module timings do not predict the complete learner ranking: miniTE with BF16 backward is slower than BF16 in seven of the eight module forward-plus-backward cells. Actual MoE execution additionally involves irregular group sizes, preparation, and scheduling. In the GB200 routing control, random weights with mock data activate 50.8 experts per layer on average, compared with 126.2 for pretrained weights and real DAPO text, out of 128. The latter workload remains strongly imbalanced across experts. The full 2 × 2 2\times 2 control in Appendix G establishes that initialization and input data change the dispatched workload. It does not decompose learner latency or assign the observed speedup to routing imbalance. The control motivates using pretrained weights and real token sequences for complete learner measurements; those measurements report the benefit of the combined numerical path and implementation.

sections.heading: Costs beyond the learner.
sections.text: Standalone NVFP4 serving reaches 80,676 output tokens/s versus 49,119 for BF16 under fixed-length generation, a 1.64 × 1.64\times gain. In a separate colocated RL window, learner time falls from 47.04 to 42.56 s, while weight conversion/synchronization rises from 9.94 to 55.26 s. The two measured stages sum to 56.98 s for BF16 and 97.82 s for miniTE (Table 13 ), identifying a weight-conversion and synchronization bottleneck. These sums omit rollout and other iteration stages and therefore do not determine whether a complete RL iteration is faster or slower. The serving comparison uses fixed-length generation and supplies a separate measure of sampling capacity. Appendix F reports these stage definitions and protocols.

sections.heading: Strict execution reference.
sections.text: The strict configuration matches learner kernels, formulas, and reduction orders to the sampler and runs without TIS. It records a log-probability difference of about 10 − 8 10^{-8} (Figure 4 ). This configuration retains native NVFP4 expert forward and BF16 gradients, and maintains reward through the region where the unaligned run deteriorates. This provides an execution-level intervention in which native FP4 computation and stable learning coexist. The practical miniTE path is evaluated separately in Figure 3 . Figure 4 : Strict execution in native NVFP4 RL. (a) Absolute learner–sampler logp difference; (b) reward, one run per configuration. Faint curves show raw values; solid curves show centered 21-step means. Strict execution jointly changes operators and omits TIS. Appendix E gives additional records.

sections.heading: Numerical preservation.
sections.text: The unfused quantization/grouped-GEMM API comparison passes all 28 bitwise checks against the upstream reference. A fused-versus-unfused layout comparison gives zero deviation in the reported synthetic and real-activation tests, including checks of externally computed amax values. These results validate the tested operand and layout transformations; Appendix D gives their shape and configuration coverage.

sections.heading: Backward precision and complete operator cost.
sections.text: Holding expert forward fixed, BF16 backward reduces directly measured forward-plus-backward latency relative to MXFP8 backward in all eight module cells, with a geometric-mean speedup of approximately 1.21 × 1.21\times . FP32-reference gradient comparisons appear in Appendix D . The backward choice also has a measured numerical effect: across the tested shapes and seeds, the largest gradient relative- L 2 L_{2} difference from the FP32 reference is 0.001663 for BF16 and 0.037653 for MXFP8. Together, the latency and gradient comparisons support choosing backward precision independently of the native W4A4 forward recipe.

sections.heading: Native low-precision learning.
sections.text: Microscaling specifies narrow elements and shared block scales ( Rouhani et al., 2023 ) . QLoRA uses four-bit storage with BF16 computation ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) , whereas Quartet executes native MXFP4 forward and gradient GEMMs ( Castro et al., 2025 ) . NVFP4 pretraining ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) , Composer 2 ( Cursor Research, 2026 ) , and Miles ( Li et al., 2026 ) provide native low-bit learning paths. Miles combines per-token NVFP4, high-precision backward, and quantizer agreement. miniTE studies residual cross-engine execution differences and the implementation cost of the native expert path.

sections.heading: Quantized RL.
sections.text: QeRL combines quantized rollout with low-rank adaptation ( Huang and others, 2025 ) ; Jet-RL unifies FP8 training and rollout ( Xi et al., 2026 ) . QUADS combines learner-side W4A16 weight QAT with sampler-side activation residual compensation ( Zhuge et al., 2026 ) . QaRL pairs low-bit forward computation with sequence-level trust-band optimization ( Gu et al., 2026 ) . miniTE evaluates native W4A4 expert-forward computation with BF16 backward and retains the existing TIS-corrected RL pipeline.

sections.heading: Execution mismatch and routing.
sections.text: Off-policy analysis ( Yao et al., 2025 ) , sequence-level ratios ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and execution-aligned references ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) examine sampler–learner consistency. FP16 studies address rounding precision ( Qi et al., 2025 ) ; selective precision ( Fedus et al., 2022 ) and routing replay ( Ma et al., 2025 ) address expert selection. Deterministic kernels control dependence on execution context ( He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ; SGLang Team, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Our diagnosis identifies residual differences under matched target-layer assignments, while the native implementation is evaluated through operator equivalence, learning traces, and complete learner timing.

sections.heading: 7  Conclusion
sections.text: Frozen-policy and routing-conditioned measurements expose execution differences beyond nominal NVFP4 agreement. We introduced miniTE , combining cross-engine diagnostics, native W4A4 forward with independently selected backward precision, and jointly optimized quantization and grouped GEMM. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, miniTE sustained learning over a long RL training horizon and outperformed standard TE NVFP4 on all four mathematics benchmarks, with a five-task average close to that of BF16. The optimized learner achieves 1.47 × 1.47\times the throughput of TE NVFP4 and 1.39 × 1.39\times that of BF16. Separate expert-forward measurements under the same recipe show a 2.46 × 2.46\times speedup over Transformer Engine. With configurable recipes, replaceable operators, and reproducible launch environments, miniTE provides an extensible foundation for numerical and systems co-design in native low-bit RL.

sections.heading: Numerical fidelity beyond execution alignment.
sections.text: Although miniTE improves mathematical evaluation over standard TE NVFP4, its practical path still falls short of BF16 in average evaluation quality and of strict execution in cross-engine agreement. Matching execution does not eliminate the quantization error associated with E2M1 values and E4M3 block scales. However, the remaining quality gap does not isolate the effects of quantization error from residual execution differences. Future work should investigate tighter execution alignment together with format-aware error compensation, aiming to improve learning quality while retaining native W4A4 computation.

sections.heading: End-to-end efficiency and hardware-aware fusion.
sections.text: Our colocated measurements identify weight conversion and synchronization as a substantial integration cost. These measurements cover selected stages rather than complete RL iterations, so component speedups alone do not establish end-to-end gains. Reducing repeated conversion and packing at learner–sampler boundaries is therefore a priority. Online amax–quantization–GEMM fusion offers a complementary direction for reducing operator-side preparation costs. Its numerical behavior and performance need joint validation, particularly when scales evolve during accumulation. Efficient implementations must coordinate scale updates, accumulator rescaling, and data movement within SM resource constraints, motivating further hardware–software co-design. Our learning evidence covers one MoE model with one run per configuration, and the implementation gains are evaluated on Blackwell hardware. Broader validation across models, tasks, independent training seeds, and hardware platforms remains future work.

sections.heading: Complete learner updates.
sections.text: Tensor, pipeline, context, and expert parallelism are respectively 1, 1, 1, and 4. Sequence length is 4,096, microbatch size is 1, and global batch size is 128, giving 524,288 tokens per optimizer update and 16 accumulation microbatches. All configurations start from the same BF16 checkpoint and seed 20260913. The input is a frozen corpus of 657 sequences of 4,097 tokens constructed from DAPO-Math-17k text, with an approximately 4.3-fold repetition factor in the construction. These are complete training updates on fixed text, with forward, backward, optimizer, and data-loading costs, rather than complete RL iterations. The interval timer synchronizes ranks and measures the slowest-rank wall time. The setup uses distributed optimization, grouped GEMM, all-to-all expert dispatch, and an FP32 router. Activation recomputation, offload, and CUDA graphs are disabled. Data indexing is cached across runs. CUTLASS NVFP4 and miniTE pad routed expert workloads to multiples of 64; the associated padding cost is included. The initial repeated experiment uses unfused MoE permutation. The optimized configuration enables –moe-permute-fusion for all variants and additionally –nvfp4-pertoken-amax-fuse for the miniTE variants, together with the dense path and GEMM-kind selection in revision b641179.

sections.heading: What an execution specification records.
sections.text: An executable numerical specification includes the quantized operands, the inner block and outer scale domains, scale dtypes and rounding, Hadamard and stochastic-rounding settings, logical layouts and padding, expert routing and packing, accumulation and epilogue precision, and the nonquantized operators surrounding the GEMM. Matching an FP4 encoding alone leaves these choices open. In miniTE , activations use length-16 blocks with E4M3 block scales and per-row FP32 outer scaling. The executed grouped path quantizes each weight output row with the same length-16 blocks and a separate FP32 outer scale per output row. The encoder clamps its row maximum as max ⁡ ( a , 10 − 12 ) \max(a,10^{-12}) before forming the global encode scale. A block whose decoded E4M3 scale is zero uses a zero encoding multiplier. The CUTLASS epilogue applies the outer scales in the order Y m ​ n = BF16 ⁡ [ 2688 − 2 ​ a n W ​ ( a m X ​ U m ​ n ) ] , Y_{mn}=\operatorname{BF16}\!\left[2688^{-2}\,a^{W}_{n}\bigl(a^{X}_{m}U_{mn}\bigr)\right], (8) where U U is the FP32 accumulator after inner-block dequantization, and a X a^{X} and a W a^{W} are the activation-row and weight-row maxima. The intermediate scale products stay in FP32 before the final BF16 rounding. The BF16-backward variant applies the straight-through estimator to the unquantized saved operands.

sections.heading: Context sensitivity of the native path.
sections.text: The context-swap test holds eight target activation rows fixed while changing the companion rows in a 128-row FC1 input. BF16 sampler activations from three prompts, of lengths 256, 512, and 1,024, are captured at layer 0, expert 79. The input and weight shapes are 128 × 2048 128\times 2048 and 1536 × 2048 1536\times 2048 ; target outputs have shape 8 × 1536 8\times 1536 . Within each case, target rows are the middle eight rows after sorting that prompt’s rows by maximum magnitude. Original companions come from the same prompt. Low- and high-amplitude replacements are selected from a pool of 2,955 captured rows across all 12 prompts. The current prompt is excluded when selecting the lowest- and highest-amplitude companions. The 256-token case has 96 companion rows and 24 zero-padding rows; the other two have 120 companions. Target positions, matrix shape, padding, and expert weights remain fixed across contexts. The per-tensor NVFP4 reference enables RHT; miniTE disables it. The reference uses a fixed 16 × 16 16\times 16 Hadamard transform and a fixed sign mask, reused across contexts. Stochastic rounding is disabled in both paths. The script does not reset the RNG between contexts; the transform is fixed by the implementation and randomly initialized module weights are overwritten with the same checkpoint expert weights. Each path therefore holds its own numerical rules fixed during the swap, although the two paths differ in RHT as well as scaling and are not a single-variable scaling ablation. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.23928v1 [cs.LG] 07 Oct 2026 miniTE : Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning September, 2026 Abstract Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39 × \times and 1.47 × \times the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning is central to large language model (LLM) post-training, supporting instruction following ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) and mathematical reasoning ( Shao et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Repeated generation, policy evaluation, and updates ( Yu et al., 2026 ) span an autoregressive sampler and a learner that optimizes on sampled sequences. Native low-precision computation must accelerate these engines while preserving effective learning. Four-bit weight storage ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) and native four-bit training ( Castro et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) address different execution paths. Quantized sampling, matched precision, and quantization-aware RL address learner–sampler mismatch ( Huang and others, 2025 ; Xi et al., 2026 ; Zhuge et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) ; recent systems also support per-token NVFP4 and high-precision backward ( Cursor Research, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . We focus on native weight-and-activation four-bit (W4A4) expert computation, connecting cross-engine diagnosis, a practical numerical path, and complete learner gains. RL makes cross-engine numerical behavior consequential. Probabilities computed by the learner and sampler enter importance ratios and clipping decisions ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) ; implementation differences therefore enter optimization even at a shared parameter version. Training–inference mismatch and execution-aligned references have been studied in RL pipelines ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) . NVFP4 adds choices in scale domains, rounding, accumulation, and operator composition that a format name does not specify. This raises a concrete question: which numerical dependencies must be exposed and controlled when native low-bit computation spans two execution engines? Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models combine continuous expert computation with discrete routing. Selective router precision and routing replay address sensitivity in expert selection ( Fedus et al., 2022 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . We examine what remains after controlling parameter updates and matching assignments at the observed layer. Frozen-policy scoring shows that NVFP4 enlarges the cross-engine log-probability tail. Target-layer routing agreement leaves FC1/FC2 output discrepancies, and a sampler-only scaling change does not establish agreement (Figure 1 ). These controls identify an execution specification, extending beyond bit width and expert IDs, as a useful unit of diagnosis and implementation. Motivated by these findings, we introduce miniTE to connect this diagnosis with practical native NVFP4 training (Figure 2 ). Our framework checks quantized operands, expert outputs, and policy evaluation across the sampler and learner. Strict execution provides a cross-engine reference for diagnosis; the default path combines our per-token quantization and native grouped-GEMM implementation with BF16 backward. Its purpose is stable, high-throughput learning under the existing RL objective. Arithmetic throughput is only one component of this cost: routed expert workloads also require operand preparation, representation conversion, and dispatch. We therefore optimize quantization and grouped GEMM as a connected dataflow, reducing repeated preparation around the numerical core so that FP4 arithmetic gains translate into faster learner updates. Comparisons between our initial and optimized operator implementations check the numerical effects of those changes. Long-horizon Qwen3-30B-A3B runs show sustained learning with miniTE and higher mathematical evaluation scores than naive NVFP4. Same-recipe module comparisons show 2.46 × 2.46\times expert-forward speedup over TE U3045. Complete learner updates on fixed text reach 1.39 × 1.39\times BF16 throughput in the optimized configuration and 1.33 × 1.33\times in a repeated core study. The module comparison measures native implementation gains; complete learner updates measure the numerical path and implementation together. Separate colocated RL measurements identify weight conversion and synchronization as an integration bottleneck. Our contributions are: 1. Execution-gap diagnosis. Frozen-policy, routing-conditioned, and scaling controls identify numerical differences beyond nominal NVFP4 recipe agreement; strict execution supplies an actionable alignment reference. 2. Practical native NVFP4 RL. An integrated W4A4 expert-forward path with BF16 backward sustains long-horizon learning and improves all four mathematics benchmarks over naive NVFP4 without modifying the RL objective. 3. A lightweight framework with numerically faithful acceleration. miniTE exposes configurable numerical recipes, replaceable expert operators, and reusable diagnostics for developing custom low-bit training settings. Operator-level numerical checks and complete learner benchmarks substantiate its execution optimizations. We release Dockerfiles, reference configurations, and single-command launch scripts to support reproducible experiments and extensions across the supported low-bit RL paths. 2 Background and Problem Setup Two executions of a policy. Let π θ L \pi^{L}_{\theta} and π θ ¯ R \pi^{R}_{\bar{\theta}} denote learner and sampler policies, with θ ¯ \bar{\theta} the sampled weight version. We introduced miniTE , combining cross-engine diagnostics, native W4A4 forward with independently selected backward precision, and jointly optimized quantization and grouped GEMM. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, miniTE sustained learning over a long RL training horizon and outperformed standard TE NVFP4 on all four mathematics benchmarks, with a five-task average close to that of BF16. The optimized learner achieves 1.47 × 1.47\times the throughput of TE NVFP4 and 1.39 × 1.39\times that of BF16. Separate expert-forward measurements under the same recipe show a 2.46 × 2.46\times speedup over Transformer Engine. With configurable recipes, replaceable operators, and reproducible launch environments, miniTE provides an extensible foundation for numerical and systems co-design in native low-bit RL. 8 Limitations and Future Work Numerical fidelity beyond execution alignment. Although miniTE improves mathematical evaluation over standard TE NVFP4, its practical path still falls short of BF16 in average evaluation quality and of strict execution in cross-engine agreement. Matching execution does not eliminate the quantization error associated with E2M1 values and E4M3 block scales. However, the remaining quality gap does not isolate the effects of quantization error from residual execution differences. Future work should investigate tighter execution alignment together with format-aware error compensation, aiming to improve learning quality while retaining native W4A4 computation. End-to-end efficiency and hardware-aware fusion. Our colocated measurements identify weight conversion and synchronization as a substantial integration cost. These measurements cover selected stages rather than complete RL iterations, so component speedups alone do not establish end-to-end gains. Reducing repeated conversion and packing at learner–sampler boundaries is therefore a priority. Online amax–quantization–GEMM fusion offers a complementary direction for reducing operator-side preparation costs. Its numerical behavior and performance need joint validation, particularly when scales evolve during accumulation. Efficient implementations must coordinate scale updates, accumulator rescaling, and data movement within SM resource constraints, motivating further hardware–software co-design. Our learning evidence covers one MoE model with one run per configuration, and the implementation gains are evaluated on Blackwell hardware.
